paras: The lynching of Frank Stone took place on the evening of July 13, 1888, near Pell City, Alabama, when a crowd of about fifty white men hanged Stone, a Black man, to a tree and riddled his body with bullets. Stone had been accused the day before of attempting to assault Mrs. Orr, a white woman, and was lynched within hours of his capture. Birmingham dispatches carried the story to papers in Memphis, Louisville, Atlanta and Ohio, and a one-line summary ran in Northern weeklies.

Pell City was a small village on the Georgia Pacific railway, about thirty miles east of Birmingham. A Birmingham special dated July 12 reported that a Black man had tried to assault Mrs. Orr, the wife of a section foreman on the railroad, near her house that day, and that her screams brought help in time. A separate dispatch credited Station Agent Mattison, who heard her screams, with stopping the attempt. That first report named the accused 'Frank Rone' and said one hundred white men were searching for him with dogs, adding that 'If caught he will be lynched without delay.'

Stone was caught about 7 o'clock on the evening of July 13 by 'a crowd of citizens', who took him at once to Pell City. He was brought before Mrs. Orr, who, the dispatch said, 'promptly identified him as the right man.' His captors then led him into the woods, where almost every man in the village joined them. A short distance into the woods he was hanged to a tree, and his body was riddled with bullets.
No report of an inquest, arrests or any official response appears in the coverage, and none of the lynchers was named.

The first notice was a single sentence among the Memphis Appeal's 'Brief Telegrams' of July 14, which placed the lynching at 'Bell City' and called the crime 'an outrage on Mrs. Orr, white.' The Atlanta Constitution printed both Birmingham specials together under the headline 'Will Go the Hemp Route', and the Weekly Courier-Journal ran the second one under 'Died on a Tree. A Negro Rapist Lynched By a Mob Near Birmingham, Alabama.' Both papers treated the accusation as established and printed the identification by Mrs. Orr as settling his guilt.

The Springfield Daily Republic in Ohio was the most openly approving, headlining its dispatch 'A Brute's Just End', calling Stone 'the brute' and 'The black fiend', and describing the lynchers as 'indignant citizens'. A syndicated weekly news summary reduced the story to one line, that Stone was lynched 'for assaulting a white woman', and ran it in Wisconsin and Minnesota papers between July 19 and 21. The Semi-Weekly Interior Journal of Stanford, Kentucky, condensed it further to 'negro—white woman—attempted rape—mob—hanging.' Every report came from the side of the pursuers, and none gave an account from Stone or from Black residents.

The Birmingham special printed in Atlanta and Louisville said Stone was caught 'near the scene of his crime.' The dispatch in the Springfield Daily Republic instead said hounds ran him down in a dense swamp five or six miles west of Seddon, where he was found hiding in a hollow log. The date also varies: the dispatches give the evening of July 13, the Courier-Journal printed the same text under a 'July 18' dateline, and the weekly summary gave 'the 14th'.

accounts.label: Birmingham special (Constitution / Courier-Journal)
accounts.gist: A crowd of citizens caught Stone about 7 p.m. near the scene, took him before Mrs. Orr, who identified him, and then fifty white men, joined by most of the village, hanged him in the woods and riddled his body with bullets.

accounts.label: Birmingham dispatch (Springfield Republic)
accounts.gist: One hundred armed and mounted men chased Stone from the time of the attempt until hounds cornered him in a hollow log in a swamp west of Seddon; he was taken back, identified by Mrs. Orr, and lynched by 'indignant citizens'.

accounts.label: Birmingham special (Memphis Appeal)
accounts.gist: A one-sentence report that Stone was lynched 'last night' at 'Bell City' for an outrage on Mrs. Orr.

framing.detail: The Springfield Daily Republic headlined the story 'A Brute's Just End' and called Stone 'the brute' and 'The black fiend'.
The Courier-Journal's 'Died on a Tree' subhead called Stone 'A Negro Rapist', treating the accusation as fact, but the body text is a plain account of the capture and lynching.
The Atlanta Constitution's headline 'Will Go the Hemp Route' over the July 12 dispatch anticipated the lynching ('If caught he will be lynched without delay').
Northern weeklies carried a one-line summary that Stone was lynched 'for assaulting a white woman', paired with the Farney item.

versions.value: Lynched the evening of July 13 (dispatch dated July 13; Memphis Appeal of July 14 says 'last night')

conflicts.note: A2's dateline is impossible for a paper dated July 16 and carries text identical to A4's July 13 dispatch; A6 is a later Northern summary. The July 13 date from the Birmingham specials is the better evidence.

conflicts.note: The two dispatches differ on where and how Stone was found; both say he was brought back to Pell City and identified by Mrs. Orr.

'Bell City' appears only in the brief Memphis telegram.

info: Lynched on the evening of July 13, 1888, the day after the alleged attempt of July 12
In the woods a short distance from Pell City, on the Georgia Pacific railway about thirty miles east of Birmingham
Accused of attempting to outrage (rape) Mrs. Orr, a white woman and wife of a Georgia Pacific section foreman; the papers say her screams brought help in time
A crowd of white citizens who captured Stone, later joined by 'almost the entire male population' of the village; none named
